pr_body:
Fixed #19959 . This follows the suggestions made by @mrdoob and @Mugen87.

Add 'glslVersion' property to ShaderMaterial and prepend the version string to the shader programs when its value is non-null.

Note: It might be best to define the glsl version strings somewhere as constants. Feel free to suggest how this should be done.
pr_comments:
I'm currently waiting for an additional review by @mrdoob since this is most likely gated by his opinion on how to best resolve #19889.

This PR does fix #19959 by requiring the `glslVersion` property for RawShaderMaterials that use the `defines` feature. This was a bug prior to #19889, so this fix can solve both issues.

The code in `WebGLProgram` should look like so:
```js
if ( parameters.isWebGL2 && ! parameters.isRawShaderMaterial ) {

	// overwrite GLSL version for built-in materials

	versionString = '#version 300 es\n';

	prefixVertex = [
		'#define attribute in',
		'#define varying out',
		'#define texture2D texture'
	].join( '\n' ) + '\n' + prefixVertex;

	prefixFragment = [
		'#define varying in',
		( parameters.glslVersion === GLSL3 ) ? '' : 'out highp vec4 pc_fragColor;',
		( parameters.glslVersion === GLSL3 ) ? '' : '#define gl_FragColor pc_fragColor',
		'#define gl_FragDepthEXT gl_FragDepth',
		'#define texture2D texture',
		'#define textureCube texture',
		'#define texture2DProj textureProj',
		'#define texture2DLodEXT textureLod',
		'#define texture2DProjLodEXT textureProjLod',
		'#define textureCubeLodEXT textureLod',
		'#define texture2DGradEXT textureGrad',
		'#define texture2DProjGradEXT textureProjGrad',
		'#define textureCubeGradEXT textureGrad'
	].join( '\n' ) + '\n' + prefixFragment;

}
```
`ShaderMaterial` requires the additional prefix code fragments. Besides, `out highp vec4 pc_fragColor;` and `#define gl_FragColor pc_fragColor` should not be defined for `ShaderMaterial` when `glslVersion` is set to `GLSL3`.

With this change, the original fiddle (https://jsfiddle.net/1q3gs0a6/1/) which works with `r118.3` also works with `dev` by just removing the GLSL version qualifier in the shader code and use `ShaderMaterial.glslVersion` instead (which is the intended migration task).

Just to clarify...

When using WebGL1, the built-in materials should use GLSL1.
When using WebGL2, the built-in materials should use GLSL3.
@mrdoob How about merging and I'll clean the above code section up? The sooner we can add this to `dev` the better  😊 .

issue_context.title: WebGL2 '#version 300 es' is not prepended when using RawShaderMaterials with 'defines' option
issue_context.body:
##### Description of the problem

When using RawShaderMaterial with the `defines` option, the `#define` definitions are prepended to the vertex/fragment program source code. However this becomes incompatible with WebGL2 shaders since the first line of these shader must be `#version 300 es`.

A proposed fix is to check for the `#version XXX` string as the first line and add the `#define` definitions after it.

##### Three.js version

- [X] Dev
- [X] r119
- [X] r118

##### Browser

- [x] All of them
- [ ] Chrome
- [ ] Firefox
- [ ] Internet Explorer

##### OS

- [x] All of them
- [ ] Windows
- [ ] macOS
- [ ] Linux
- [ ] Android
- [ ] iOS

##### Hardware Requirements (graphics card, VR Device, ...)
comments:
For reproduction: https://jsfiddle.net/hns8etfr/

BTW: This did not work in earlier version, too (it's unrelated to #19889).
I guess this will be a bit hacky to solve since the engine expects that`#version 300 es` is defined in user code.

I'm going to need a solution to this since another open source project relies on the defines to readjust the shaders dynamically, and that project can't upgrade to WebGL2 shaders without this change. 

I'll send a PR with the proposed solution: check the user program for the `#version 300 es` and append the defines after it.
@Mugen87 thanks for the quick work with that!

I heard that using GLSL 1 in WebGL 2 may be buggy.

So, I think it may be better if the renderer added `#version 300 es` to `RawShaderMaterial`s by default (so you don't have to). And in cases that you need GLSL 1 then you can force WebGL 1 by doing `new THREE.WebGL1Renderer()`.

Would that work?

> Would that work?

Basically yes. But since users already have `#version 300 es` in their shader code, they would have to perform a migration task. Otherwise the qualifier is added twice (which produces a shader which does not compile).  #19965 avoids a breaking change though.

> #19965 avoids a breaking change though.

Yes, but it also complicates the code... 😕

I think it's fair to change this now even if it's a breaking change. It's pretty early days for this code path.

I've tested to always add `#version 300 es` on my system but encountered a problem. Consider the code in:

https://threejs.org/examples/webgl_buffergeometry_rawshader

It's GLSL 1 code. If the engine should enforce GLSL 3.0 for `RawShaderMaterial`, the following code must be executed otherwise the shader won't compile:

https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/1213e0f8a73f6cb9e74be0c04ba6730da423c3a0/src/renderers/webgl/WebGLProgram.js#L675-L703

So the fix would be remove the `! parameters.isRawShaderMaterial` check. Do you think it's okay if this code (meaning the GLSL 1.0 to 3.0 conversion) is also executed for `RawShaderMaterial`?
Hmm, the fix for that particular case should be to use `new THREE.WebGL1Renderer()` in the example.

Oh wait, it seems #19889 indeed had an effect. Check out this code:

`r118.3`: https://jsfiddle.net/1q3gs0a6/1/

A custom `ShaderMaterial` written with GLSL 3.0. Notice how it's required to define `outColor` since `gl_FragColor` can't be used. After #19889, GLSL version qualifiers are defined twice and two out colors are defined which breaks the code.

`r119.1`: https://jsfiddle.net/1q3gs0a6/2/

I've realized this when try to remove `! parameters.isRawShaderMaterial`.

> Hmm, the fix for that particular case should be to use new THREE.WebGL1Renderer() in the example.

Okay. So the policy would be:

- A `RawShaderMaterial` with GLSL 1.0 code has to use `WebGL1Renderer`.
- A `RawShaderMaterial` with GLSL 3.0 code has to use `WebGLRenderer` (and thus WebGL 2). The GLSL version qualifier is added by the engine.

Does that sound right?

> Does that sound right?

Yes, that's the idea. Sounds manageable to me.

Just for the record: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/issues/19959#issuecomment-667214812 does not work since engine code using `RawShaderMaterial` (like PMREM) needs to work with WebGL 1 and 2. Thus exclusively using GLSL 3.0 in context of `RawShaderMaterial` and WebGL 2 does not work. GLSL 1.0 must be supported, too. Otherwise we need two version of PMREM shaders.

@mrdoob and @Mugen87 could have a look at PR #20005? It should cleanly handle the prepending and solve this bug for new code changes without breaking existing code.

To summarize, for GLSL 3.0 shaders, the `glslVersion` property of the ShaderMaterial should be set. This will apply the version string correctly to the top of the file. If it is not set, then no action is taken. It is assumed the shader code accounts for the version number in this case. This is independent of the gl version of the context so any version of GLSL can be used in the shader code.

The Harp.gl has modified their code to support WebGL2 and they are waiting for this bug to be resolved. See [this PR](https://github.com/heremaps/harp.gl/pull/1756). Will you review and merge PR #20005 to solve this bug?

I've tested your PR in detail today and provided feedback here: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/pull/20005#issuecomment-674378445

Implementing the suggested code should make the PR ready to merge.

review_comments: I suggest to introduce two new constants `THREE.GLSL1` and `THREE.GLSL3` and use the former one as the default value of `glslVersion`.

I've left the default as null. This is required to apply the conditional GLSL 3.0 logic to the internal shaders. This seems to be the least invasive way to fix support for GLSL 3.0 in new code without breaking old code.

@mrdoob should review this line. To summarize: if the default `glslVersion = null` is used then backwards compatibility is retained for users not using this new feature. If `glslVersion = GLSL1` is used then a forced migration task is required for all RawMaterialShaders that use `#version 300 es`, those programs will break.
